findings.claim: Arati is "the waving of a flame (typically in a multi-wicked lamp called a thali or aarti dish) before a murti".
findings.truth: A thali is the metal tray on which the lamp and offerings are placed; it is not the lamp. The lamp is a diya or multi-wicked deepak carried on the thali. The lesson also drifts to the spelling "aarti" here while using the spec form "arati" everywhere else.
findings.evidence: Standard description of arati; spec 3.1.4.2 lists the term as 'arati'

findings.claim: "Over 3,000 volunteers helped during its construction" (BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir, Neasden).
findings.truth: About 450 craftsmen, 100 full-time volunteers and over 1,000 part-time volunteers worked on the mandir.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir London

findings.claim: Flashcard answer: the Neasden mandir is "the largest Hindu temple outside India".
findings.truth: It was the largest Hindu mandir outside India when it opened in 1995, but later BAPS mandirs have surpassed it. The lesson body already calls it the largest Hindu temple in Europe; the flashcard must match.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir London

findings.claim: "The mark scheme requires you to name a sacred writing or source of authority."
findings.truth: The instruction comes from the question stem, not from a mark scheme. House rule bans mark-scheme claims and board descriptor wording.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1; CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC copyright-distancing rule

findings.claim: "naming sub-traditions earns marks".
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. No mark is awarded for naming a sub-tradition; naming one only helps the student show the range of Hindu practice.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1 (1, 1, 4, 6, 12 structure; no such rule)

findings.claim: "The GCSE specification identifies five main focuses of Hindu worship", followed by a list of six items; the key fact then lists a different five that drops the murti.
findings.truth: The specification gives five: the many deities, guru and other elders; one God (personal or non-personal); holy land, hills and rivers; sacred plants and animals; the murti as a representation of God. Deities and guru are one bullet, and the murti is one of the five.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.4.2, 'Focuses of worship and representations of the divine'

findings.claim: "Most Hindus are vegetarian, in part because of ahimsa..."
findings.truth: A minority are. The Pew Research Center 2021 survey of India found 44% of Hindus identify as vegetarian, with wide regional variation (71% in the north, 18% in the east).
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Vegetarianism in India (Pew Research Center, 2021)

findings.claim: "Guru Brahma, Guru Vishnu, Guru Devo Maheshwara" is glossed as "The guru is Brahma, the guru is Vishnu, the guru is Shiva - to the guru I bow."
findings.truth: The translation includes the second line of the shloka, which is not quoted. The full verse is "Guru Brahma, Guru Vishnu, Guru Devo Maheshwara; Guru sakshat param Brahma, tasmai shri gurave namah". Quote the whole verse or trim the translation.
findings.evidence: The Guru shloka (Guru Gita); internal mismatch between quotation and translation

findings.claim: "The specification distinguishes between personal and non-personal focuses of worship."
findings.truth: The specification applies 'personal or non-personal' only to the bullet 'one God'. It does not sort every focus of worship into personal and non-personal. The distinction belongs to Hindu practice, not to the specification's structure.

findings.claim: Bhagavad Gita quoted with no chapter or verse: "In whatever way people are devoted to me, in that same way I fulfil their desires."
findings.truth: This renders Bhagavad Gita 4.11 ('ye yatha mam prapadyante'). The 6-mark question requires a named source, so the reference should be given.
findings.evidence: Bhagavad Gita 4.11; spec 4.4.1

findings.claim: Leicester "has one of the largest Hindu populations outside India" and its Belgrave Road Diwali "attract[s] hundreds of thousands of visitors each year".
findings.truth: Leicester is 17.9% Hindu (2021 census), roughly 66,000 people - one of the largest Hindu communities in Britain, but far from one of the largest outside India (Greater London, Kathmandu, Durban and many others are bigger). No source supports hundreds of thousands of visitors; tens of thousands is the safe figure. Wikipedia does support the stronger claim that the Belgrave Road celebrations are the largest of their kind outside India.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Leicester (2021 census) and Belgrave, Leicester

findings.claim: The four yogas are "four paths to moksha described in the Bhagavad Gita".
findings.truth: The Bhagavad Gita sets out karma, jnana and bhakti yoga. The eight-limbed astanga path is described in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras. The lesson's own key fact says this, so the conclusion contradicts the body.
findings.evidence: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali; internal contradiction with the lesson key fact

findings.claim: "Diversity of practice is a mark-scheme reward."
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. House rule bans mark-scheme claims and board wording.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1; CHECK_PROMPT_GENERIC copyright-distancing rule

findings.claim: The charity is named three ways in one lesson: "Sewa International UK" (key fact), "The Sewa UK charity" (body) and "Sewa UK" (conclusion and flashcard); it is called "inspired directly by the Vedic principle of service".
findings.truth: The UK body is Sewa International UK. Students must learn one name for a named organisation. Seva is a Hindu principle of service; it is not a specifically Vedic term.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Sewa International ('Sewa International UK chapter')

findings.claim: Every lesson opens its practice set with a question typed "1 mark - Multiple Choice" (L1 Q1, L2 Q1, L3 Q1, L4 Q1).
findings.truth: The specification fixes the marks (1, 1, 4, 6, 12) but says nothing about question style, so this cannot be settled from the spec alone. Either AQA's 1-mark items are open recall, in which case all four should be relabelled '1 mark' and rewritten as short-answer prompts, or a multiple-choice 1-marker is fine as a house drill. The marks themselves are valid. Recommendation: leave the items but settle the label fleet-wide for AQA RS A, because the same pattern runs through every religion unit.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1 (marks only, no question-style guidance)
findings.ruling: Leave: label fleet-wide / titles unverified this session.

findings.claim: "The Hindu Climate Declaration (2015), to which many British Hindu organisations are signatories..."
findings.truth: The 2015 document is titled 'Bhumi Devi Ki Jai! A Hindu Declaration on Climate Change', released before COP21 and coordinated by the Bhumi Project; an earlier Hindu Declaration on Climate Change came out of the 2009 Parliament of the World's Religions. 'The Hindu Climate Declaration' is not its title. Wikipedia has no article on it and the Bhumi Project pages returned 404, so I could not confirm the title or the signatory claim within the fetch budget. Recommendation: rename it 'the Hindu Declaration on Climate Change (2015)' and soften the signatory claim to 'supported by Hindu organisations in Britain and worldwide'.
findings.evidence: WebFetch: Hindu_Declaration_on_Climate_Change 404, Hinduism_and_environmentalism silent, bhumiglobal.org 404
findings.ruling: Leave: label fleet-wide / titles unverified this session.

findings.claim: "organisations such as the Hindu Forum of Britain work to address domestic violence and gender inequality within and beyond the Hindu community."
findings.truth: The Hindu Forum of Britain is real - an umbrella body for UK Hindu groups founded in December 2003 - but its recorded work is advocacy on religious freedom and community representation. No source I could reach records domestic-violence or gender-inequality work. The spec strand asks for charities that promote well-being, social inclusion and women's rights, so a wrong named example is worse than none. Recommendation: drop the attribution and say that British Hindu community and temple groups run projects supporting women, or replace it with a charity Tom can verify.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Hindu Forum of Britain
findings.ruling: Leave: label fleet-wide / titles unverified this session.

findings.claim: Named individuals are quoted as real witnesses: Nalini, 52, of Coventry (L1); Meena, 72, of Leicester and Dev, 19 (L3).
findings.truth: These people are invented and their words are invented, but the text presents them as reported testimony. Nothing they say is factually wrong, so no edit is proposed. Worth a house decision on whether vignettes should be marked as illustrative.
findings.evidence: internal - no source cited for any quotation

findings.claim: "over 40 million pilgrims attended a single day of the 2019 gathering at Prayagraj".
findings.truth: True but dated. The 2019 event was an Ardh Kumbh; the 2025 Maha Kumbh at Prayagraj was far larger. The figure is not wrong, so it is left alone.
findings.evidence: widely reported 2019 peak-day figures

findings.claim: Vivekananda's combining of the four paths "is sometimes called 'integral yoga'".
findings.truth: Integral yoga is Sri Aurobindo's term. Vivekananda taught a harmony or synthesis of the four yogas. The text hedges with 'sometimes called', so no edit is proposed.
findings.evidence: standard usage of the term

summary: Fourteen fixes across all four lessons: two invented examiner claims, a wrong volunteer count and an out-of-date superlative for the Neasden mandir, a miscounted specification list, the false claim that most Hindus are vegetarian, an over-stated Leicester Hindu population, a half-quoted guru shloka, an unreferenced Gita quotation, astanga yoga wrongly credited to the Gita, and three names for one charity. All marks used (1, 4, 6, 12) are valid for this specification and no lesson names the board, a spec code or a band descriptor. Three items need Tom's ruling: the multiple-choice 1-mark house format, the title of the Hindu climate declaration, and the Hindu Forum of Britain women's-rights claim.
